Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 45
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Agricultural Worker
  trauma_type: Witnessed domestic violence (childhood)
  pcl5: 48

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Never Alone: make sure never to be alone with another person, Rumination: Revenge: ruminate about how to get even with assailant, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma
  Threat: Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard, Night Vigilance: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day, Cannot Trust Safety: Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Happiness: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable., Lost Faith: I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power, Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened

Vignette:
Kofi Mensah is a 45-year-old Ghanaian-born agricultural worker who has lived in the rural American South for the past twelve years, working the long seasonal cycles of a large produce farm. He came to his first appointment quietly, sitting with his hands folded in his lap and choosing his words with visible care. What brought him in, he said finally, was that he had not slept a full night in longer than he could remember, and his partner of seven years had told him, plainly and with evident pain, that she no longer recognized who he was.

The event Kofi carries happened when he was nine years old, in a two-room house in the outskirts of Accra. His father was a man who drank and, when he drank, became someone else entirely. On the night Kofi remembers most vividly, he stood in the narrow doorway between the rooms and watched his father beat his mother with sustained and methodical force. He was close enough to see her face turn toward him — not to ask for help, he has always told himself, but simply because he was there. He did not move. He did not shout. He pressed himself into the doorframe and he watched, and when it was over he went back to his mat and lay still in the dark. His mother recovered. Nothing was ever said. But Kofi has never, in thirty-six years, forgiven himself for standing in that doorway and doing nothing. He will never forgive himself, he says, with a certainty that sounds less like guilt and more like a sentence he has already accepted.

In the years that followed, the memory did not disappear so much as it went underground, surfacing in forms he did not immediately connect to that night. By the time he was working the fields in Georgia and South Carolina, patterns had formed in his life that felt, to him, simply like reasonable precautions. He had come to believe that people were fundamentally unknowable and dangerous — that the man who seemed calm was only a version of his father before the drinking started. He had lost whatever faith he once held in the idea that life moved toward goodness. He described himself, with a kind of flat accuracy, as someone who used to laugh easily and now found happiness something that happened to other people.

At work, Kofi is rarely alone with any single coworker. He arranges himself near groups, moves when the configuration of the field leaves him one-on-one with another man, and has developed a reputation among the crew for being standoffish — a reputation that has cost him a crew-leader position he was informally offered and then quietly withdrawn. He does not explain himself. He simply ensures that there is always someone else nearby. When he returns to the small house he shares with his partner in the evenings, the nights are their own kind of difficulty. He lies awake long after she has fallen asleep, alert to sounds from outside, unable to settle into anything that feels like safety. When she has told him he is safe, that they are fine, that nothing is wrong, he has heard her words and felt nothing shift inside him. He cannot make himself believe it, and he knows she has noticed.

He has spent years trying not to think about the doorway, about his mother's face, about what a different version of himself might have done. The effort of not thinking about it occupies him more than he would like to admit. In the spaces where the suppression fails — late at night, during the slow monotony of fieldwork — his mind moves instead toward a dark and circular fantasy of confrontation, of what it would mean to make his father answer for what he did. His father has been dead for eleven years. The rumination continues regardless.

What finally brought Kofi to seek help was his partner's face — the particular tiredness in it — and the recognition that he was, in some measurable way, disappearing from his own life. He came in hoping, he said quietly, that there might be some way to stop carrying the doorway with him everywhere he goes. What he feared most was that there wasn't.
